title: RFID & NFC Case Studies — Real Proud Tek Deployments by Industry
summary: Documented Proud Tek RFID and NFC deployments — hotel locks, industrial laundry, festival access, retail apparel, library self-service and pharmaceutical traceability. Each case lists the customer profile (anonymised where required), the procurement constraints, the chip and form factor selected, the volume shipped and the operational results measured after go-live. Use these pages to short-list a chip family and form factor that has already shipped against a workflow comparable to yours.
keywords: RFID hotel key card case study
heroPoints: Six documented deployments spanning hospitality, industrial laundry, events & venues, retail apparel, library systems and pharmaceutical traceability — between 50,000 and 2,400,000 units per program per year.

Each case study lists the chip family selected (MIFARE Classic 1K, MIFARE DESFire EV3, NTAG215, NTAG424 DNA, {chip:impinj-monza-r6-p:name}, {chip:nxp-ucode-8:name}) and why competing chip families were rejected for the workflow.

All results are measured numbers — chargeback avoidance, shrink reduction, inventory accuracy, read-rate after 50 wash cycles, encoding throughput, lead time — taken from joint go-live reviews with the customer's operations team.

paragraphs: Every case study follows the same structure: customer profile and constraints, chip and form factor selected, alternatives considered and why they were rejected, MOQ and lead time delivered, the measured operational result after the deployment went live and the next-step CTA. Reading three or four cases adjacent to your workflow surfaces the practical trade-offs faster than reading the product datasheet in isolation.
bullets: Hospitality — Multi-property hotel group switching from magnetic-stripe key cards to MIFARE Classic 1K key cards across 28 properties.
Industrial laundry — Uniform rental operator deploying PPS RFID laundry tags rated for 300-500 wash cycles.
Events & venues — Music festival access control with UHF RFID wristbands cashless-payment ready.
Retail apparel — Source-tagged hang tags on {chip:impinj-monza-r6-p:name} inlays for store inventory accuracy.
Libraries — Library self-service migration onto {chip:nxp-icode-slix2:name} book labels and AFI security.
Pharmaceuticals — DSCSA-compliant item-level RFID labels for a US specialty pharmacy distributor.

sections.title: How to read these cases for your own procurement
sections.intro: The fastest way to take value from a case study is to map your project onto the four constraints we list at the top of every page.
bullets: Frequency band — LF 125 kHz vs HF 13.56 MHz vs UHF 860–960 MHz. The frequency forces 80% of the downstream chip and reader decisions.
Read range and environment — pocket-distance (1–5 cm) vs hand-held (3–10 cm) vs lane / portal (1–10 m). Metal, water and human-body interference shape antenna and form-factor choice.
Volume and lifecycle — single-use vs multi-use vs permanent. A festival wristband and a hospital patient wristband have similar form factors but radically different chip-cost envelopes.
Compliance regime — hotel brand standard, GS1 EPC, DSCSA, FDA UDI, EU DPP. The compliance regime dictates encoding format, label artwork and audit trail.

faq.question: Are the case-study customer names real?
faq.answer: We disclose the customer name where the customer has given Proud Tek written permission to do so. Where the customer has asked to remain unnamed (typically retail chains, hotel groups under brand-standard NDAs and US pharmaceutical distributors), we describe the customer profile with enough specificity that a procurement reader can recognise an analogue without identifying the underlying brand. Volume figures, chip part numbers, lead times and operational results are always real.

faq.question: Can I speak to one of these customers as a reference?
faq.answer: Yes, subject to a short NDA and a written request. Reference calls are coordinated by your Proud Tek account manager, typically scheduled within 5–10 business days. We ask buyers to provide a one-paragraph project brief in advance so the reference call covers the procurement questions that actually matter to your shortlist.

faq.question: Why are some volumes shown as ranges (e.g. 200k–500k / year) rather than exact figures?
faq.answer: Annual volume in a stable programme is rarely flat — there are launch peaks, replenishment troughs and seasonal cycles. Where the customer's volume varies more than 15% year-over-year, we publish a range that brackets the last two complete fiscal years. This is more honest than picking a single high-water number.

faq.question: Do you have a case study for [my industry] that is not listed here?
faq.answer: Almost certainly yes — Proud Tek has shipped product into more than 30 verticals. The six published case studies are the ones with the strongest documentation and customer permission to share. For unpublished verticals (agriculture, education, fitness, automotive tire OEM, data-center IT asset tracking, cold-chain food traceability, government & defense supply chain) please contact the team for a private deployment brief that mirrors the same structure.

faq.question: What is the typical sample-to-PO timeline for a programme like the ones in these case studies?
faq.answer: Across the six published cases the median was 6–10 weeks from first sample request to first production PO. The path is: sample pack (5–10 business days FOB Shenzhen) → spec sign-off (1–3 weeks of engineering iteration) → pre-production sample (2–3 weeks) → first PO (2–4 week production lead time depending on volume). Volumes above 1 million units / year often add a tooling-amortisation step that extends the front-loaded portion by 2–4 weeks.

faq.question: Can Proud Tek match the price points referenced in these case studies for a smaller buyer?
faq.answer: Within a band, yes — production economies of scale flatten beyond the 100,000-unit mark for most SKUs, so a 100,000-unit / year buyer typically lands within 15–25% of a 1,000,000-unit / year buyer's unit price. Below 50,000 units / year the per-unit cost ladder steepens, but Proud Tek still serves smaller buyers through a shared-tooling SKU programme where the chip, antenna and lamination are stock and only the printed artwork and encoding are project-specific.
